lesson.title: What Makes Something Fit in a For Loop
lesson.summary: An object is iterable if it implements __iter__ and that method returns an iterator, which is exactly what a for loop asks for behind the scenes before it starts looping.
lesson.body:
You have written for item in some_list: many times, and it has always just worked, whether some_list was a list, a string, a dictionary, or a range. That is not because for loops have special-cased knowledge of each of those types. It is because each of them implements a dunder method called __iter__, and the for loop's entire job description is short: call __iter__() on whatever comes after in, and repeatedly pull values from whatever __iter__() returned, until there are no more.

An object that implements __iter__ correctly is called an iterable. Being iterable does not mean the object tracks its own position or knows how to produce its "next" value by itself, it only means that when asked, it can hand back a separate object, called an iterator, that does know how to do that. The simplest way to implement __iter__ on a class you write is to delegate to an iterable you already have.

```python
class Deck:
    def __init__(self, cards):
        self.cards = cards

    def __iter__(self):
        return iter(self.cards)

deck = Deck(["A", "K", "Q"])
for card in deck:
    print(card)
```

This prints:

A
K
Q

Deck.__iter__ does not build anything new, it calls the built-in iter() function on self.cards, which is a plain list, and returns whatever iterator that list already knows how to produce. The for loop never touches deck.cards directly, it only ever calls deck.__iter__() once, at the start, and then repeatedly asks the returned iterator for the next value.

It is worth being precise about the vocabulary here, because the next chapter builds directly on the distinction. Iterable describes any object with a working __iter__ method, meaning it can be handed to a for loop, or passed to iter(), or unpacked, or passed to functions like sorted() and list(). Deck, above, is iterable. It is not, itself, an iterator, because it has no way to be asked "what's next" directly, it can only produce something else that can answer that question. The next chapter shows what a class looks like when it plays that second role itself.
